Table 23. AssistOS-specific terms



Term or aspect Meaning or practical use AssistOS The overall platform and ecosystem for creating, supervising and collaborating with persistent virtual workers. Robot A persistent, personalized virtual worker with a role, agent configuration, home, task history and private sandboxed execution environment. Robot home Durable role-specific state comparable in spirit to a Linux home directory; it may include configuration, caches and a browser profile. RoboTeam A configured group of Robots working for an individual or team. Explorer The plugin-capable web workspace that exposes projects, files, tools, Robots and collaboration surfaces. WebChat The AssistOS Copilot and conversational dispatch surface. WebMeet The collaborative meeting environment where people and Robots can share screens, chat and modify shared state. Ploinky The deployment/runtime system for packaged capabilities. Ploinky Agent A deployable capability package; it may contain an AI Agent, tools, services or a complex containerized application. Task A bounded unit of Robot work with state, inputs, outputs, limits and history. Project The durable workspace in which artifacts, tasks and collaboration accumulate.



The most important distinction to retain is the one among Robot, AI Agent and Ploinky Agent. A Robot is the persistent worker a user delegates to. An AI Agent is reasoning-and-action software. A Ploinky Agent is a deployable capability package that may contain an AI Agent, tools or both. Many public documents use “agent” more broadly; the narrower vocabulary is a product-design choice intended to make the user model stable.

heading: General AI and software terms
text:
Table 24. General AI and software terms



Term or aspect Meaning or practical use AI Agent Software that can pursue a goal by reasoning, choosing actions and using tools on behalf of a user or another program. Large Language Model (LLM) A neural language model trained on large text corpora and used for generation, analysis and other language tasks. Container An isolated user-space runtime that packages software and its dependencies while sharing the host kernel. Sandbox A restricted execution environment intended to limit what a program can read, write or affect. API A defined software interface through which one program requests data or actions from another. Model Context Protocol (MCP) An open standard for connecting AI applications to external data sources, tools and workflows. OpenAI-compatible API An API that imitates commonly used OpenAI request/response conventions so existing clients can integrate with another service. WebRTC A family of browser and real-time communication technologies for direct audio, video and data exchange. Local-first A design preference that keeps useful data or computation under local control when practical while still allowing remote services. Model neutrality The ability to replace or route among AI models without rebuilding the user’s whole work environment. Provenance Information about where an artifact came from and which inputs, processes or actors produced it. Least privilege The security principle of granting only the permissions necessary for the intended function.



These terms are not unique to AssistOS. The recommended links in the bibliography and glossary point to introductory references rather than assuming that a reader already knows systems engineering vocabulary. A student should be able to read the main chapters first and use the appendix only when a term becomes a barrier.

heading: Appendix B Architecture at a glance
text: The architecture supports one continuing relationship among people, Robots and projects, from an individual installation to a managed organization.

heading: The smallest useful architecture
text:
A minimal AssistOS installation can be described without a large distributed-systems diagram. The user opens Explorer. WebChat acts as Copilot and dispatch surface. One or more Robots exist as persistent worker identities with homes and task history. Each Robot can use one or more Ploinky Agents. Ploinky starts those capabilities in controlled runtimes. Projects provide the files and artifacts on which work occurs.







Figure 6. AssistOS architecture at a glance. The product can scale from one machine to managed infrastructure without changing the basic user model.



Figure 6 compresses the architecture into four visible levels. The top is interaction: Explorer, WebChat and WebMeet. The next is the Robot layer, where roles, homes and tasks live. The next is the Ploinky capability layer, where packaged agents and tools run. The bottom is execution infrastructure: the host operating system, containers or lighter sandboxes, local services and optional remote resources. The architecture can grow, but the user story does not need to change.



The main design rule is continuity across replaceable parts. A Robot can survive a restarted container. A project can survive a changed model. A plugin can be replaced without destroying project files. A Ploinky Agent can be upgraded while the task history records which version produced earlier work. This separation is what allows AssistOS to evolve without requiring users to rebuild their working identity every few months.

heading: A company deployment
text:
A company deployment adds policy around the same core. An organizational catalog determines which Ploinky Agents can be enabled. Identity connects humans and Robots to projects. Secret management supplies scoped credentials. Network policy constrains external access. Administrators can inspect task histories and revoke capabilities. Shared servers or workstations can provide execution capacity while Explorer remains the common interface.



Table 25. What an enterprise adds to the same Robot model



Term or aspect Meaning or practical use Organizational identity Connects human users and Robot identities to approved projects and roles. Capability catalog Defines which Ploinky Agents and versions can be installed in managed environments. Secrets service Provides scoped credentials without storing every secret as a normal file in Robot homes. Policy layer Controls project access, network destinations, approval thresholds, model providers and budgets. Execution pools Provide managed workstations or servers while preserving the same Robot and task model. Audit and telemetry Record significant actions, package versions, costs, failures and administrative interventions.



The table shows that enterprise scale is primarily an addition of governance, not a different product concept. This matters commercially because the individual and enterprise experiences can share the same mental model. The individual user learns to create a Robot, give it a task and inspect results. The company adds rules about which Robots, tasks and capabilities are allowed.

heading: Appendix C Questions for adoption
text: These questions help turn the ideas in the handbook into an assessable first workflow and deployment.

heading: Questions for a first workflow
text:
A prospective user should not begin by asking which model is strongest. They should begin with the workflow. What work is being delegated? What files or systems are involved? Which actions are reversible? Where does human judgment enter? What constitutes successful output? If these questions cannot be answered at all, the task may be too vague for reliable automation.



Table 26. Questions for a first AssistOS workflow



Term or aspect Meaning or practical use Workflow What recurring digital work do we want the Robot to perform? Inputs Which files, websites, applications or data sources are actually required? Reversibility Which mistakes can be undone easily, and which actions are consequential? Credentials Can the Robot use a scoped identity rather than a human user’s unrestricted credentials? Human checkpoint Where should the Robot deliberately pause for judgment or authorization? Output What artifact or evidence demonstrates that the task was completed? Success metric How will we measure cycle time, human effort, errors and intervention? Cost boundary What model or compute budget is acceptable per useful task? Exit plan Can the project, artifacts and configuration be exported if the platform or model changes?



The questions in the table can be used in a pilot workshop. They are deliberately phrased in ordinary language. Technical details such as container runtime, MCP transports and model routing can be decided afterward. This ordering keeps the platform focused on the human problem.

heading: Questions for an organization or investor
text:
A company or investor should additionally ask whether the product can be deployed and governed repeatedly. Can a capability be packaged once and installed consistently? Can the organization restrict which projects a Robot can access? Can a Robot be stopped? Can its browser identity be revoked? Can the same project survive a model change? Can the team measure task success and intervention? Can third-party capabilities be evaluated before use?



Early prototypes can demonstrate interaction and architecture. Production claims require reliability measurements, security testing and real deployment evidence. A buyer should establish which features are available in the proposed installation and which remain development or research directions.
